items.title: Dual ball as a closed subset of a product
items.statement: Evaluation embeds the closed dual unit ball of a real or complex normed X homeomorphically as a closed subset of the product of scalar disks D_x={z:|z|<=||x||}.
items.strategy: The subspace product topology is weak-star. Additivity and scalar homogeneity are closed equations; the coordinate bounds imply boundedness and norm<=1. All equations together characterize the image. Treat X={0} as well. Compactness of finite-dimensional scalar disks must use an earlier local result.

references.title: Bühler–Salamon, Functional Analysis (2017), §3.2.3, Theorem 3.33, pp. 134–135
Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis (2017), §5.3, proof of Theorem 5.10, pp. 146–147

items.title: Banach alaoglu
items.statement: Assume the ultrafilter lemma. The closed dual unit ball of every real or complex normed space is compact in the weak-star topology.
items.strategy: Each scalar disk is compact Hausdorff. Use the ultrafilter lemma exactly for compact-Hausdorff Tychonoff, then pass to the closed image from the preceding lemma. Completeness of X is not used.

references.title: Bühler–Salamon, Functional Analysis (2017), §3.2.3, Theorem 3.33, pp. 134–135
Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis (2017), §5.3, Theorem 5.10, p. 147

items.title: Absolute polar in a normed dual pair
items.statement: For U subset X, U^circ consists of f in X* satisfying |f(u)|<=1 for every u in U.
items.strategy: Fix the absolute-value polar convention over both scalar fields; distinguish one-sided real polars.

references.title: Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis (2017), Problem 5.3, p. 141

items.title: Weak star compactness of polar sets
items.statement: If U is a norm neighborhood of zero in X, its absolute polar U^circ={f in X*: |f(u)|<=1 for every u in U} is weak-star compact under the ultrafilter lemma.
items.strategy: Define the absolute polar explicitly before its use. Since U contains rB_X for some r>0, its polar lies in r^(-1)B_X*. It is an intersection of closed evaluation constraints. Scaling the dual ball and closed-subset compactness give the result; U need not be convex or balanced.

references.title: Bühler–Salamon, Functional Analysis (2017), §3.2.3, Theorem 3.33, pp. 134–135
Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis (2017), Problem 5.3, p. 141, and §5.3, Theorem 5.10, p. 147

items.title: Dual ball weak star metrizable for separable predual
items.statement: Given a fixed dense sequence (x_n) in a normed X, on each norm-bounded subset of X* the weak-star topology is induced by d(f,g)=sum_(n>=1) 2^(-n) min(1,|(f-g)(x_n)|).
items.strategy: Dense evaluations separate by the common norm bound. Control the series tail and finitely many evaluations in one direction; approximate finitely many arbitrary test vectors by the supplied dense sequence in the other. The boundedness restriction is essential; a metric on the whole dual is not claimed.

references.title: Bühler–Salamon, Functional Analysis (2017), §3.2.1, proof of Theorem 3.30, p. 132
Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis (2017), §5.3, formula (5.12), pp. 146–147

items.title: Separable banach dual ball is weak star sequentially compact
items.statement: Assume the ultrafilter lemma. Every sequence in the closed dual unit ball of a separable normed space has a weak-star convergent subsequence.
items.strategy: The ball is compact and metrizable; apply the published ZF implication from compact metric to sequentially compact. Completeness is unnecessary.

references.title: Bühler–Salamon, Functional Analysis (2017); exact harvest in batch coverage
Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis (2017); exact harvest in batch coverage

items.title: Goldstine
items.statement: Assume HB. For every real or complex normed space X, J_X(B_X) is weak-star dense in B_(X**).
items.strategy: For finite tests map B_X into scalar finite-space. If the bidual value vector misses the compact convex closure, the earlier Euclidean strict point/closed-convex separation theorem, expressed as the real part of a scalar-linear combination, gives Re x**(f)>||f||. HB is used through bidual norming, not compactness.

references.title: Bühler–Salamon, Functional Analysis (2017), §3.1, Corollary 3.29, pp. 131–132
Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis (2017), §5.3, Theorem 5.13, pp. 148–149

items.title: Goldstine finite data approximation
items.statement: Assume HB. For x** in B_(X**), finitely many f_j in X*, and epsilon>0, there is x in B_X with |f_j(x)-x**(f_j)|<epsilon for every j.
items.strategy: Unpack weak-star density in the bidual. This is a single finite-data existence assertion, not a selection of approximants for all data.

references.title: Bühler–Salamon, Functional Analysis (2017), §3.1, Corollary 3.29, pp. 131–132
Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis (2017), §5.3, Theorem 5.13, pp. 148–149

items.title: Banach dieudonne linear subspace criterion
items.statement: Assume the ultrafilter lemma, DC, and HB. For a real or complex Banach space X and a linear subspace E of X*, E is weak-star closed iff E intersect B_(X*) is weak-star closed.
items.strategy: Bühler–Salamon Theorem 3.40/Corollary 3.41, pp138–141, gives the full finite-test induction. A convergent sequence in E is bounded; rescale it into the weak-star closed E∩B* to prove E norm closed, so d=dist(f0,E)>0. Fix 0<δ<d. Inductively choose finite S_n⊂B_X such that no f∈E with ||f-f0||≤δ(n+1) passes all earlier tests max_{x∈S_k}|(f-f0)(x)|≤kδ (1≤k<n) and the new test max_{x∈S_n}|(f-f0)(x)|≤nδ. If every candidate finite S passed, these closed test sets would have the finite-intersection property in the weak-star compact bounded slice E∩(||f||≤||f0||+δ(n+1)); their common f would have ||f-f0||≤nδ and pass every earlier test, contradicting the induction hypothesis at n. DC chooses successive S_n. Enumerate all S_n/n in finite blocks (padding by zero if needed) as a norm-null sequence x_i. For f∈E choose n≥max(2,||f-f0||/δ); the induction property at n gives k<n and x∈S_k with |(f-f0)(x)|>kδ, hence ||Tf-Tf0||∞>δ for T:X*→c0, Tf=(f(x_i)). Thus dist(Tf0,T(E))≥δ. HB separates Tf0 from the closure of T(E); c0*=ℓ1 supplies β with ||β||1=1, β∘T=0 on E, and |β(Tf0)|≥δ. Normalize α_i=β_i/β(Tf0); the absolutely convergent Banach series x0=Σα_i x_i has ||x0||≤δ^-1, f0(x0)=1, and E(x0)=0. This weak-star separates f0 from E. For complex X, identify its complex dual isometrically with the real dual of X viewed as a real Banach space by f↦Re f, inverse g↦(x↦g(x)-i g(ix)); real and complex weak-star topologies agree because evaluating at x and ix recovers both components. Apply the real argument to the realification of E. The ultrafilter lemma supplies Alaoglu compactness, DC the recursive choices, and HB the c0 separation; the declared HB supplier itself carries its own AC contract.

Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis (2017); exact harvest in batch coverage

items.title: Extreme point and face
items.statement: For a real convex set K in a real or complex vector space, x is extreme if x=ty+(1-t)z, y,z in K, 0<t<1 implies y=z=x. A face F is a nonempty convex subset of K satisfying the analogous endpoint property.
items.strategy: Distinguish arbitrary faces from exposed faces and from extremal subsets, which need not be convex. Use the missing LCS prerequisite pair to establish the ambient topology before the compact theorems.

Hanche-Olsen, Topological vector spaces, p. 13

items.title: Minimizer face of a continuous affine functional
items.statement: A real-valued continuous affine functional on a nonempty compact convex K attains its minimum; the minimizers form a nonempty compact face. Faces of faces are faces.
items.strategy: Scalar compactness gives attainment. Affinity proves the endpoint property, continuity closedness, and convexity follows from equality at the minimum. Verify transitivity directly.

Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis (2017); exact harvest in batch coverage

items.title: Krein milman existence of extreme points
items.statement: Under AC, every nonempty compact convex subset K of a locally convex Hausdorff topological vector space has an extreme point.
items.strategy: Order nonempty compact faces by reverse inclusion. FIP makes each chain intersection a nonempty compact face; Zorn gives a minimal face. If it has two points, the published separating-dual theorem, with HB supplied from AC, gives a proper nonempty minimizing face.

references.title: Bühler–Salamon, Functional Analysis (2017); exact harvest in batch coverage
Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis (2017); exact harvest in batch coverage

items.title: Krein milman closed convex hull form
items.statement: Under AC, a compact convex subset K of a locally convex Hausdorff space is the closed convex hull of its extreme points; allow empty K with empty hull.
items.strategy: For nonempty K, separate any point outside the closed convex hull of ext(K) from that hull by a continuous real functional. Its maximizing face in K has an extreme point by existence, which is extreme in K by transitivity, contradicting separation. The hull is closed inside compact K.

items.title: Upper semicontinuous real map on a topological space
items.statement: For a topological space T, a map f:T to R is upper semicontinuous when every strict sublevel {x:f(x)<a} is open, equivalently every superlevel {x:f(x)>=a} is closed; this agrees with the existing pointwise definition on subspaces of R.
items.strategy: Record the topological convention needed by Bauer before its use. The equivalence is by complements, and agreement with the earlier real-domain definition is the published level-set characterization.

references.title: Ian Ball, Bauer’s Maximum Principle for Quasiconvex Functions, p. 1

items.title: Bauer maximum principle
items.statement: Under AC, a real-valued upper-semicontinuous convex function on a nonempty compact convex subset K of a locally convex Hausdorff space attains its maximum at an extreme point of K.
items.strategy: Upper semicontinuity and compactness show the nonempty maximum set M is closed and compact: the closed superlevel sets at levels approaching the supremum have the finite-intersection property. Convexity makes M extremal but not necessarily convex: x^2 on [-1,1] has M={-1,1}. Order nonempty compact extremal subsets of M by reverse inclusion; intersections are extremal and compact. A separating functional on a nonsingleton minimal subset cuts a proper compact extremal subset by maximizing; therefore it is a singleton extreme in K. This is the standard proof in Ball pp1–2, not an invalid invocation of KM on M. Inline extremal-subset definition and its transitivity are required.

items.title: Milman converse for compact generating sets
items.statement: If K is compact convex in a locally convex Hausdorff space, A subset K, and K=closed convex hull(A), then ext(K) subset closure(A). In particular a compact generating A contains ext(K).
items.strategy: Hanche-Olsen Theorem 22 pp13–14. For extreme w outside closure(A), choose a convex zero-neighborhood U with (w+U-U) disjoint from closure(A). Cover compact closure(A) by finitely many x_j+U. Let K_j be closed convex hull((x_j+U) intersect closure(A)); these lie in K and avoid w since their preclosures avoid the open w+U. The convex hull of the finite union K_j is compact via the simplex times their finite product and equals K. A finite convex representation of extreme w forces every positive-weight point to equal w, contradicting avoidance. Do not claim closure(co(A)) compact for arbitrary compact A without the assumed compact K.

items.title: Dual unit ball has extreme points
items.statement: Assume AC. The closed unit ball of the dual of every nonzero real or complex normed space has an extreme point.
items.strategy: The weak-star topology is locally convex Hausdorff by finite evaluations; Alaoglu gives compactness. Apply Krein–Milman. Combined implemented cost is AC, never the ultrafilter lemma alone. Historical converse KM plus the ultrafilter lemma=>AC remains unverified pending Bell full text and must not serve as a dependency.

title: Banach Alaoglu Goldstine and Krein Milman — Examples

items.title: Weak star compactness of probability measures
items.statement: For compact Hausdorff K, regular Borel probability measures form a compact subset of C(K)* for convergence against continuous functions, under the ultrafilter lemma plus the representation suppliers.
items.strategy: For compact Hausdorff K, C_c(K)=C_0(K)=C(K). The published real positive and complex regular-measure representation theorems identify probabilities with positive normalized functionals. Positivity is the intersection of the weak-star closed inequalities f(g)>=0 over nonnegative real-valued g, and normalization is f(1)=1. Positivity gives norm one when K is nonempty, so this is a weak-star closed slice of the dual ball; for empty K the set is empty and compact. Alaoglu contributes exactly the ultrafilter lemma.

references.title: Bühler–Salamon, Functional Analysis (2017), §3.2.2, pp. 133–134, and §3.2.3, Theorem 3.33, pp. 134–135
Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis (2017), §5.3, Theorem 5.10, p. 147

items.title: Extreme points of the probability measures are dirac masses
items.statement: For compact Hausdorff K, the extreme regular Borel probability measures are exactly the Dirac masses.
items.strategy: If 0<mu(A)<1 for a Borel A, the two normalized restrictions supplied by the restriction theorem split mu nontrivially. A finite regular measure restricted to Borel A remains regular: inner compact approximation is immediate, while a compact C subset A with mu(A\C) small makes K\C an open neighborhood of K\A of small restricted mass, giving outer approximation. Conversely, suppose every Borel set has mass zero or one. The family of closed full-measure sets has the finite-intersection property, so compactness gives a common point x. Every neighborhood of x has full measure. A compact C disjoint from x has a neighborhood disjoint from some neighborhood of x by compact Hausdorff separation, hence mu(C)=0; inner regularity gives mu(K\{x})=0. Thus mu=delta_x. Dirac masses are extreme because positive summands in a convex decomposition vanish off {x} and have total mass one.

references.title: D. H. Fremlin, Measure Theory, Volume 4, Chapter 43, §437S, Proposition, p. 73

items.title: Extreme points of the ell infinity unit ball
items.statement: Extreme points of the closed ell^infinity unit ball are exactly sequences with |x_n|=1 for every n (real signs or complex unit-circle coordinates).
items.strategy: An interior disk coordinate admits a small symmetric perturbation. Conversely equality at a boundary coordinate in a convex combination in the scalar disk forces equality of both coordinates there; do this at every n.

items.title: The c0 unit ball has no extreme points
items.statement: The closed unit ball of c0 has no extreme points over either scalar field.
items.strategy: For any x in that ball, choose a coordinate with |x_n|<1; sufficiently small positive real perturbations plus and minus at that coordinate stay in the ball and in c0. They are distinct and average to x.

items.title: C0 is not isometrically a dual space
items.statement: Under AC, c0 is not linearly isometric onto the dual of any normed space.
items.strategy: A surjective linear isometry identifies the closed unit balls and preserves extreme points. Contradict the preceding two items. The stronger isomorphic statement remains assigned to the later compact-operator track.

items.title: Weak star compact does not imply weak star sequentially compact
items.statement: The weak-star compact unit ball of (ell^infinity)* need not be sequentially compact.
items.strategy: The norm-one coordinate evaluations Lambda_n(x)=x_n lie in it. For any subsequence with increasing indices n_k, prescribe x_(n_k)=(-1)^k and x_j=0 otherwise. This x in ell^infinity makes the evaluated subsequence divergent. Hence no subsequence is weak-star convergent. Compactness uses the ultrafilter lemma; the obstruction is explicit.

items.title: Banach alaoglu versus sequential alaoglu
items.statement: Alaoglu compactness, separable bounded-ball metrizability, and sequential compactness have distinct hypotheses and proof costs.
items.strategy: Record the ultrafilter lemma for Alaoglu and for the separable corollary via the choice-free compact-metric tail proof; AC for the implemented KM combination. Retain the Bell pp59–64 historical KM plus the ultrafilter lemma=>AC obligation as BLOCKED, not an approved recorded assertion. Rossi is Stefano Rossi; its equivalence discussion is orientation only.

items.title: Reflexive iff unit ball weakly compact
items.strategy: The canonical map identifies the weak topology with the relative weak-star topology on its range. Surjectivity transfers Alaoglu compactness. Conversely the compact image of B_X is weak-star closed and Goldstine-dense in B_X**, hence equal. The ultrafilter lemma is used only by Alaoglu in the forward direction; HB is used by the relative bidual isometry and Goldstine.
items.statement: Assume the ultrafilter lemma and HB. A real or complex Banach space is reflexive iff its closed unit ball is weakly compact.

items.title: A banach space is reflexive iff its dual is reflexive
items.strategy: If J_X is onto, represent F in X*** by F composed with J_X. Conversely J_X(X) is closed by completeness under AC_omega, and any annihilator F is evaluation by f in X*; vanishing on all J_Xx forces f=0, hence F=0. Annihilator separation proves density. HB supplies separation and bidual isometry; AC_omega supplies complete-subspace closedness. No Alaoglu is needed.
items.statement: Assume HB and AC_omega. A real or complex Banach space X is reflexive iff X* is reflexive.

items.title: Closed subspaces of reflexive spaces are reflexive
items.strategy: For y** compose with restriction X*->Y*. Reflexivity represents the composite by x. Annihilating Y-perp forces x in Y; surjectivity of restriction then proves y**=J_Yx. HB supplies extension/separation; no compactness shortcut is required.
items.statement: Assume HB. Every closed subspace of a real or complex reflexive Banach space is reflexive.

items.title: Quotients of reflexive spaces are reflexive
items.strategy: Identify (X/Y)* with Y-perp, extend a functional on Y-perp to X* using HB, represent it by x, and verify its quotient representative is x+Y. AC_omega is used by the published quotient-completeness theorem; HB supplies norm-preserving extension. Do not assert that the quotient map carries the closed unit ball onto the quotient closed unit ball.
items.statement: Assume HB and AC_omega. Every quotient of a real or complex reflexive Banach space by a closed subspace is reflexive.

items.title: Complex Lp duality from real Lp duality
items.statement: Assume countable choice. For 1<p<infinity, every bounded complex-linear functional on complex Lp over any measure space is uniquely integration against a complex Lq density in the bilinear pairing, with equality of norms.
items.strategy: Restrict to real-valued Lp and represent the real and imaginary parts by real Lq densities a,b. Complex linearity gives density a+ib. Complex Holder gives boundedness; the phase test |h|^(q-2) conjugate(h), with zero convention, gives norm equality and uniqueness.

items.title: Reflexivity of lp for one less p less infinity
items.strategy: Apply the real or complex representation theorem at p and its conjugate q, then verify that the composite density identification is the canonical bidual map under the bilinear pairing.
items.statement: Assume countable choice. For every measure space and 1<p<infinity, real and complex Lp are reflexive.

items.title: Relative weak compactness and three sequential notions
items.strategy: Use Haase, EFHN Appendix E.5 pp353–356, as the accessible alternate treatment. Define relative compactness as compactness of the weak closure in X; relative sequential compactness means every sequence has a weakly convergent subsequence with its limit in X; relative countable compactness means every indexed sequence has a weak cluster point in X, i.e. every neighborhood contains terms with arbitrarily large indices. For absolute versions require the resulting point in A. This indexed convention handles finite and eventually constant sequences correctly; the empty set satisfies all relative conditions. The definitions require only the declared weak-topology supplier and no unavailable source proof.
items.statement: For A in Banach X, relative weak compactness means weak closure in X is weakly compact; relative weak sequential compactness means every sequence in A has a weakly convergent subsequence with limit in X; relative weak countable compactness means every sequence in A has a weak cluster point in X (every neighborhood contains infinitely many indexed terms). Absolute versions require the limits or cluster points in A. Empty A satisfies the three relative conditions.

items.title: Eberlein smulian separable reduction
items.strategy: Enumerate rational (Gaussian rational in the complex case) finite linear combinations by an explicit enumeration of finite natural strings; no countable union choice is used. Hahn-Banach makes restriction X*->Y* onto, so the intrinsic weak topology and the relative weak topology have the same finite-coordinate tests. To avoid the published Mazur theorem's unpropagated AC dependency, apply the relative HB geometric-separation theorem directly to any point outside the norm-closed linear span; the separating functional gives a weak neighborhood disjoint from the span. Closed-subspace completeness makes the span Banach. This reduction alone does not prove Eberlein-Smulian.
items.statement: Assume HB. For a sequence in X, its closed scalar span Y is a separable Banach subspace. Its weak topology is the relative weak topology inherited from X, and Y is weakly closed.

items.title: Eberlein smulian metrization on the relevant dual ball
items.strategy: Use the owner-approved accessible Haase Appendix E.2 metrization pattern, specialized to a weakly compact subset. From separability, canonically enumerate a dense subset of the unit sphere (handling Y=0 separately). Under AC_omega choose, for each dense unit vector, an HB norming functional. The resulting countable family separates points. Its evaluation map sends K continuously and injectively into the countable scalar product. Equip each scalar coordinate with min(1,|s-t|); scalar completeness and the standard weighted-product lemma give a metric inducing the product topology. The compact-to-Hausdorff theorem makes the evaluation map a homeomorphism onto its metric subspace. This does not metrize all of Y or weakly compact subsets of nonseparable spaces, and it uses no claim from the unavailable Whitley paper.
items.statement: Assume countable choice and HB. A weakly compact subset K of a separable normed space Y is weakly metrizable: a countable norming family in Y* gives a continuous injection of K into a countable scalar product, hence a homeomorphism onto its image.

items.title: Countable compactness closes in the bidual
items.statement: Assume the ultrafilter lemma, DC, and HB. If A in a Banach space is relatively weakly countably compact, then A is norm bounded and the weak-star closure of J_X(A) in X** is contained in J_X(X).
items.strategy: Use the complete alternative route in Haase, EFHN Appendix E, Lemma E.1 and Theorems E.2–E.3 and E.14, pp345–347 and 354–356; do not claim Whitley's inaccessible induction. Let K=B_{X*} with weak-star compact Hausdorff topology (Alaoglu under the ultrafilter lemma) and Φ:X→C(K), Φ(x)(f)=f(x). HB makes Φ isometric, and its pointwise topology on Φ(X) is exactly the weak topology of X. A weakly countably compact A is norm bounded: if f(A) were unbounded, DC on finite valid histories would produce |f(a_n)|>n, contradicting a weak cluster; then apply UBP to {J(a):a∈A} on the Banach dual X*, whose completeness follows from bounded-operator-space completeness. Every sequence in Φ(A) has a pointwise cluster in Φ(X), so Φ(A) is relatively countably compact in C_p(K). Prove Grothendieck E.14 directly: the pointwise closure B of Φ(A) is contained in a compact product of bounded scalar disks by compact-Hausdorff Tychonoff; if g∈B is discontinuous at y, choose ε>0 with y in the closure of Z={z:|g(z)-g(y)|≥ε}. Use DC on finite valid histories to choose f_n∈Φ(A) approximating g at y and prior x_m, shrink nested neighborhoods U_n of y by compact-Hausdorff regularity, and choose x_n∈U_n∩Z. Relative countable compactness gives a pointwise cluster f∈Φ(X) of f_n, while the finite-intersection property of the closed tail closures gives a cluster x of x_n in compact K. For each n, x lies in cl U_n, giving f(x)=g(y); for each m, f(x_m)=g(x_m). Continuity of f at the cluster x contradicts |g(x_m)-g(y)|≥ε. Thus B⊂C(K). To show B⊂Φ(X), prove E.3 without Haase's implicit arbitrary selection: for each positive n,m use the full finite-coordinate open cover of K^n indexed by all h∈Φ(A); compactness gives a nonempty finite subcover, and DC selects these finite subcovers over paired countable indices. Their union A0 is countable and g lies in its pointwise closure. The pointwise closure P of A0 is compact and separable. Prove E.2 for P: a dense sequence of functions and the standard countable-product scalar metric induce a continuous pseudometric on K; DC selects finite pseudometric nets and their explicitly enumerated union gives evaluation points. The tail-closure compactness argument of E.1 transfers convergence from the dense functions to every function in P, so those evaluation points separate P. The resulting continuous injection of compact P into a countable scalar product is a homeomorphism onto its metrizable image. Hence a least-index construction gives a sequence from A0 converging pointwise to g. Its weak cluster a∈X exists by hypothesis, and pointwise uniqueness gives g=Φ(a). Therefore every x** in weak-star closure J(A) restricts on K to such a g=Φ(a); scaling all f∈X* gives x**=J(a). All countable selections use DC through explicit finite-history relations; no arbitrary indexed choice is inferred. The scalar/complex argument uses absolute values throughout.

items.title: Eberlein smulian
items.strategy: First derive AC_omega locally from DC by applying DC to the entire one-step-extension relation on finite partial choice histories; do not consume the unproved implication merely stated in the choice definitions. Compact-to-sequential: for any sequence in relatively weakly compact A, take its weakly closed separable closed span Y and intersect it with the weak compact closure of A. Closed-in-compact makes the intersection compact, the intrinsic and relative weak topologies agree, and the existing AC_omega+HB metrization lemma plus the choice-free compact-metric implication gives a weakly convergent subsequence. Sequential-to-countable uses convergence plus growth of strictly increasing subsequence indices. Countable-to-compact: the preceding Haase/Grothendieck bidual-closure lemma proves A bounded and D=cl_w* J(A) lies in J(X). Alaoglu applied to X* and continuous scalar multiplication make the scaled bidual ball compact; a direct finite-evaluation closure estimate puts D in that ball, and closed-in-compact makes D compact. The evaluation identity makes J:X_weak→J(X)_weak-star a homeomorphism under HB, and the subspace closure calculation gives D=J(cl_w A); the continuous inverse image is therefore compact. All three implications cover both scalar fields and empty, zero and zero-radius cases. The unavailable Whitley induction is replaced by the complete Haase route, not cited as read.
items.statement: Assume the ultrafilter lemma, DC, and HB. Relative weak compactness, relative weak sequential compactness, and relative weak countable compactness are equivalent in a real or complex Banach space.

items.title: Reflexive iff every bounded sequence has a weakly convergent subsequence
items.strategy: Assume the ultrafilter lemma, DC and HB, matching the two selected suppliers. First prove the norm-closed unit ball is weakly closed using one HB norming functional at each exterior point. If X is reflexive, the compact-ball criterion makes B_X weakly compact and Eberlein-Smulian makes it relatively weakly sequentially compact; divide a bounded sequence by one positive bound, treating bound zero separately, and rescale its weakly convergent subsequence. Conversely, the bounded-sequence property makes every sequence in B_X have an ambient weakly convergent subsequence. Eberlein-Smulian makes B_X relatively weakly compact, and weak closedness makes this actual weak compactness; the compact-ball criterion gives reflexivity. Record exactly that BPI enters the forward compact-ball theorem, DC enters Eberlein-Smulian, and HB enters norming and both main suppliers.
items.statement: Assume the ultrafilter lemma, DC, and HB. A real or complex Banach space is reflexive iff every norm-bounded sequence has a weakly convergent subsequence in the space.

items.title: Schur property
items.strategy: Definition concerns sequences only; it does not identify the weak and norm topologies.
items.statement: A Banach space has the Schur property when every weakly convergent sequence converges in norm.

items.title: Ell one has the schur property
items.strategy: Reduce to a weakly null sequence. If its norms do not tend to zero, use the well-ordering principle and natural-number recursion to take the least later norm-large indices and least finite cutoffs giving small old heads and new tails. One bounded sign sequence in the real case, or conjugate-phase sequence for the complex no-conjugation pairing, has a uniformly large pairing with every chosen vector, contradicting weak nullity. The deterministic least-index recursion adds no choice.
items.statement: Real and complex ell-one have the Schur property.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis (2017)

items.title: Ell one is not reflexive
items.strategy: Assume the ultrafilter lemma, DC and HB, as required by the bounded-sequence reflexivity criterion. Coordinate unit vectors have norm one and mutual distance two. If ell-one were reflexive, that criterion would give a weakly convergent subsequence; Schur would make it norm convergent and hence Cauchy, contradicting the distance calculation. The Schur supplier itself is choice-free.
items.statement: Assume the ultrafilter lemma, DC, and HB. Neither real nor complex ell-one is reflexive.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis (2017)
references.locator: Discussion and example following Theorem 4.30, printed pp. 128–129

items.title: Uniformly convex banach space
items.strategy: State the unit-ball version; distinguish it from strict convexity and from invariance under equivalent renorming.
items.statement: A Banach space is uniformly convex if for each epsilon in (0,2] there is delta>0 such that ||x||,||y||<=1 and ||x-y||>=epsilon imply ||(x+y)/2||<=1-delta.

references.title: Haim Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations

items.title: Uniform convexity gives unique asymptotic centers
items.strategy: Take a bounded minimizing sequence of centers. Radius zero is Cauchy by the triangle inequality. For positive radius, normalize two good centers by a common radius and use uniform convexity at their midpoint to force Cauchyness. Completeness, closedness and the 1-Lipschitz radius give existence; the same estimate gives uniqueness.
items.statement: Assume countable choice. For a bounded sequence in a uniformly convex Banach space, the asymptotic radius function r(y)=limsup_n||x_n-y|| has a unique minimizer on each nonempty closed convex subset.

references.title: Teck-Cheong Lim, On Asymptotic Centers and Fixed Points of Nonexpansive Mappings
references.locator: §§1–2, especially Proposition 1 and Theorem 1, printed pp. 421–423

items.title: Milman pettis
items.strategy: First transfer the uniform-convexity estimate from B_X to B_X**: a fixed almost-norming dual test preserves the separation of u** and v**, while a second arbitrary dual test controls their midpoint through two independent finite-data Goldstine approximants. Now fix z in S_X** and epsilon>0. Choose an almost-norming f in B_X* and, by Goldstine, x in B_X with Re f(x) close to Re z(f). The midpoint of z and Jx lies too near the bidual unit sphere for their distance to exceed epsilon. Scaling makes J_X(B_X) norm dense in B_X**. Under countable choice, the relative HB bidual isometry and completeness make J_X(X) closed, so J_X is onto. The ultrafilter lemma is not used.
items.statement: Assume HB and countable choice. Every real or complex uniformly convex Banach space is reflexive.

references.title: Haim Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations
Harald Hanche-Olsen, Topological vector spaces

items.title: James nonreflexivity sequence separated from an annihilator
items.strategy: Megginson §1.13 Theorem 1.13.14(a)→(b), with the separable construction in Theorem 1.13.11(a)→(b), supplies the exact interface. Because X is nonreflexive, its closed ball is not weakly compact by the local ultrafilter-lemma/HB reflexivity criterion; Eberlein–Šmulian (the ultrafilter lemma, DC, HB) gives a bounded sequence with no weakly convergent subsequence. Its closed linear span M is separable and nonreflexive: if M were reflexive, a subsequence would converge weakly in M and hence in X by restriction/relative HB, contradiction. Closedness makes M Banach. The canonical image J(M) is a proper norm-closed subspace of M** by the bidual isometry and completeness. Riesz separation (prove the standard one-line quotient-unit-ball argument here) gives F in B_M** with dist(F,J(M))>theta. Choose a dense sequence (m_j) in M; this is the DC/countable-choice use already declared. For K_n={u* in M*:u*(m_j)=0 for j<=n}, the finite-dimensional annihilator span{Jm_1,...,Jm_n} satisfies ||F|K_n||=dist(F,span{Jm_1,...,Jm_n})>theta. Prove this equality inline: the <= direction is immediate; extend F|K_n norm-preservingly by relative HB, and the difference annihilates K_n, hence lies in the finite span. Choose u_n* in B_{K_n} with F(u_n*)>theta, then scale to F(u_n*)=theta. These individual successive choices use DC. For every finite convex combination u* of u_n*, F(u*)=theta, so ||u*||>=theta; each u_n*(m_j)=0 for n>=j, and density plus ||u_n*||<=1 gives u_n*(m)→0 for all m∈M. Extend each u_n* from M to x_n*∈B_X* via relative HB; this countable dependent construction uses DC. For any x*∈co{x_n*} and w*∈M^perp, restriction to M is a convex combination of the u_n*, so ||x*−w*||>=theta. The zero space cannot enter because it is reflexive. Do not infer the conclusion from separable James alone without this extension-and-annihilator separation.
items.statement: Assume the ultrafilter lemma, dependent choice, and the relative Hahn–Banach principle. If a real Banach space X is not reflexive, then for each theta in (0,1) there are a separable closed subspace M of X and a sequence (x_n*)_{n in N} in the dual unit ball such that x_n*(m) tends to 0 for every m in M and dist(M^perp, co{x_n*:n in N})>=theta, where M^perp={w* in X*:w*(M)=0}.

references.title: Robert E. Megginson, An Introduction to Banach Space Theory (1998)

items.title: James convex-block norm-attainment criterion
items.strategy: This is Megginson Lemma 1.13.13 and Theorem 1.13.14(b)→(d), specialized to A=B_X. First prove L(s_n*) is nonempty for any bounded sequence by dominated HB on the sublinear p(x)=limsup_n s_n*(x); its members have norm <=sup||s_n*||. Convex-block selection V(s_n*) consists of sequences v_n*∈co{s_j*:j>=n}; then L(v_n*)⊂L(s_n*), and taking subsequences retains the inclusion. With T_n=sum_{j>=n}beta_j, choose errors e_n>0 tending to 0 with sum_n beta_n e_n/(T_n T_{n+1})<1−theta. Set (0x_n*)=(x_n*). At induction step m, after y_1*,...,y_{m−1}*, define α_m as the infimum over y*∈co{(m−1)x_j*:j>=m} and v∈V((m−1)x*) of the supremum over w*∈L(v) of ||sum_{j<m}beta_j y_j*+(sum_{j>=m}beta_j)y*−w*||. The candidate set is nonempty by dominated HB, all norms are <=2, and the separation hypothesis yields α_1>=theta. Nested convex-block tails and the displayed normalized convex combination in Megginson Claim 4 give α_{m−1}<=α_m<=2. Choose y_m*, a block sequence (mz_j*), and w_m*∈L(mz*) within relative error e_m so α_m(1−e_m)<||sum_{j<m}beta_j y_j*+(sum_{j>=m}beta_j)y_m*−w_m*||<α_m(1+e_m). Choose a unit-ball witness x_m for the strict lower inequality; use a subsequence (mx_j*) of (mz_j*) whose evaluations on x_m tend to the liminf. All dependent recursive choices use DC. The block/subsequence inclusions imply L(y*)⊂intersection_m L(mx*)⊂intersection_m L(mz*); hence the same x_m witnesses the lower bound for every w*∈L(y*). The upper bound follows from the selected supremum, so letting m→infinity gives ||sum beta_j(y_j*−w*)||=α=lim α_m∈[theta,2]. Iterating the exact identity P_n=(beta_n/T_n)Q_n+(T_{n+1}/T_n)P_{n-1} and telescoping beta_n/(T_nT_{n+1}) proves the strict prefix bound. Finally use geometric weights and split the series at an arbitrarily late index whose evaluation lies below the liminf threshold. Under the additional ultrafilter lemma, the preceding noncompactness lemma gives L(x_n*)⊂M^perp and the required distance for every nonreflexive X.
items.statement: Assume dependent choice and the relative Hahn–Banach principle. For a real Banach space X, theta in (0,1), and a zero-based dual-ball sequence (x_n*) with dist(L(x_n*),co{x_n*:n in N})>=theta, where L(x_n*)={w* in X*:w*(x)<=limsup_n x_n*(x) for every x in X}, every positive weight sequence beta_n summing to 1 admits alpha in [theta,2] and a zero-based dual-ball sequence (y_n*) such that for every w* in L(y_n*), ||sum_{j>=0} beta_j(y_j*−w*)||=alpha and ||sum_{j=0}^n beta_j(y_j*−w*)||<alpha(1−theta sum_{j>n}beta_j) for every n in N. In addition, assuming the ultrafilter lemma, if X is nonreflexive then some bounded linear functional fails to attain its norm on B_X.

references.title: Robert E. Megginson, An Introduction to Banach Space Theory (1998)

items.title: James reflexivity theorem
items.strategy: If X is reflexive, norm-preserving HB extends the norm-one functional on span{f} inside X*; surjectivity of the canonical map represents that bidual functional by a unit-ball vector where f attains its norm. Conversely, if real X is nonreflexive, the preceding James convex-block criterion constructs z* with |z*(x)|<||z*|| for every x∈B_X, contradicting universal attainment. For complex X, realify to X_R. Every real bounded u on X_R has complexification f(x)=u(x)−i u(ix) with ||f||=||u||. If f attains its norm at x, rotate x by a unit complex scalar so u attains ||u|| there. The real James result makes X_R reflexive. To prove complex reflexivity rather than merely cite it, extend a complex bidual F to the real-dual correspondence by U(u)=Re F(f_u), represent U by x using real reflexivity, and recover both real and imaginary parts of F(f)=f(x) by testing f and if. Explicitly retain the ultrafilter lemma, DC, HB assumptions used in the local prerequisite chain; X={0} satisfies both sides.
items.statement: Assume the ultrafilter lemma, dependent choice, and the relative Hahn–Banach principle. A real or complex Banach space is reflexive iff every bounded scalar-linear functional attains its norm on the closed unit ball, including the zero space.

references.title: Robert E. Megginson, An Introduction to Banach Space Theory (1998)

items.title: Quantitative Bishop–Phelps support functional construction
items.strategy: Use the maximizing Ekeland construction, proved inline, on the complete metric subspace C (closedness plus completeness of X). For 0<eta<epsilon choose x0 in C with f(x0)>sup_C f−eta; this is an individual choice from the defining supremum. For a continuous bounded-above real function F on a complete metric space define S(x)={y:F(y)>=F(x)+eta d(x,y)}. Each S(x) is nonempty and closed. Under dependent choice, recursively choose x_{n+1} in S(x_n) with F(x_{n+1})>sup_{S(x_n)}F−2^(−n). Transitivity gives nested S(x_n). The increase F(x_{n+1})−F(x_n)>=eta d(x_n,x_{n+1}) and boundedness above make the sequence Cauchy; its limit v belongs to all S(x_n). For z in S(v), transitivity puts z in every S(x_n), so F(z)<=F(x_{n+1})+2^(−n), hence F(z)<=F(v). The defining inequality for S(v) forces z=v. Thus F(x)<F(v)+eta||x−v|| for x≠v and F(x)<=F(v)+eta||x−v|| for all x in C. This is the only DC use. Now take F=f|C and D=union_{t>=0}t(C−v), a convex cone because C is convex. For d=t(c−v), f(d)<=eta||d||. Define p(x)=inf_{d in D}(eta||x+d||−f(d)). It is finite: triangle inequality and the preceding cone bound give p(x)>=−eta||x||, while d=0 gives p(x)<=eta||x||. Cone addition and positive scaling make p sublinear, and p(0)=0. Apply the published relative HB dominated-extension theorem to the zero functional on {0}, obtaining h in X* with h(x)<=p(x); the bounds on p(x),p(−x) give ||h||<=eta. For d in D, p(−d)<=−f(d), hence h(d)>=f(d). Put g=f−h; then ||g−f||<=eta<epsilon and g(c−v)<=0 for every c in C. Thus g attains its supremum at v. This is the exact support-cone interface used by the next theorem; no undefined subgradient or generic separation assertion is imported.
items.statement: Assume dependent choice and the relative Hahn–Banach extension principle. Let C be a nonempty closed bounded convex subset of a real Banach space X. For every f in X* and every epsilon>0 there are v in C and g in X* with ||g-f||<=epsilon and g(x)<=g(v) for all x in C.

references.title: Philip D. Loewen and Xianfu Wang, A Generalized Variational Principle, Canadian Journal of Mathematics 53 (2001), 1174–1193
references.locator: PDF pp.4–5, Theorem 2.2 and inequality (2.14), and PDF pp.15–16, Proposition 5.1(i) and Theorem 5.2

items.title: Bishop phelps
items.strategy: Given f in X* and epsilon>0, apply the quantitative support-functional lemma to obtain g with ||g−f||<epsilon and g(v)=sup_C g. This gives norm density. For C=B_X, symmetry gives sup_B g=||g||, hence real norm attainment. Explicitly retain the DC and relative-HB assumptions from the construction. For a complex Banach space, realify and apply the real theorem on the same unit ball to Re f. The supporting real functional u has unique complexification U(x)=u(x)−i u(ix), with ||U−f||=||u−Re f||. Since the complex unit ball is balanced, u(v)=sup_B u=||u||=||U||; Re U(v)=||U|| and |U(v)|<=||U|| force U(v)=||U||. No complex general-convex-set assertion is made.
items.statement: Assume dependent choice and the relative Hahn–Banach extension principle. For every nonempty closed bounded convex subset C of a real Banach space X, continuous real-linear functionals attaining their supremum on C are norm dense in X*. In particular, real norm-attaining functionals are dense for the unit ball. For a complex Banach space, complex-linear functionals attaining their norm on its closed unit ball are also norm dense; no general complex convex-set analogue is asserted.

references.title: Philip D. Loewen and Xianfu Wang, A Generalized Variational Principle, Canadian Journal of Mathematics 53 (2001), 1174–1193
references.locator: PDF pp.4–5, Theorem 2.2 and inequality (2.14), and PDF pp.15–16, Proposition 5.1(i) and Theorem 5.2

items.title: Separable dual implies separable primal
items.strategy: Handle X={0}. For a dense sequence f_n choose x_n in the unit ball with |f_n(x_n)|>=||f_n||/2 (take x_n=0 when f_n=0). Any functional annihilating their span has arbitrarily small norm by approximation with f_n. HB annihilator separation gives density; rational or Gaussian rational span gives countability.
items.statement: Under countable choice and the relative Hahn–Banach extension principle, if the continuous dual of a real or complex normed space X is norm separable, then X is norm separable.

items.title: Separable reflexive space has separable dual
items.strategy: J_X identifies X** with X, making X** separable; apply the preceding theorem to X*. Separability of X alone does not suffice.
items.statement: Under countable choice and the relative Hahn–Banach extension principle, a separable reflexive Banach space has separable dual.

items.title: Clarkson inequalities in both exponent ranges
items.strategy: For p≥2 put r=p/2≥1. The complex parallelogram identity gives |a+b|²+|a−b|²=2(|a|²+|b|²); use u^r+v^r≤(u+v)^r≤2^{r−1}(u^r+v^r) to obtain |a+b|^p+|a−b|^p≤2^{p−1}(|a|^p+|b|^p), then integrate. For 1<p≤2 set q=p/(p−1)≥2. Prove the scalar two-point estimate (|a+b|^q+|a−b|^q)^{1/q}≤2^{1/q}(|a|^p+|b|^p)^{1/p} without a later complex-analysis theorem. The full elementary source is Kuriyama–Miyagi–Okada–Miyoshi, Theorems 2.5 and 3.2, pp120–123. For real nonnegative a≥b, normalize a=1 and t=b/a. Their Theorem 2.5 studies F(t)=((1+t)^q+(1−t)^q)^{1/q}/(1+t^p)^{1/p}. With q conjugate to p, the derivative sign is that of G(t)=(1+t)^{q−1}(1−t^{p−1})−(1−t)^{q−1}(1+t^{p−1}); Lemmas 2.1–2.4 prove G is first negative and then positive for q>2, so F has its maximum at t=0 or 1. Both endpoint values are 2^{1/q}. For complex a,b, rotate common phase and write b/a=re^{iθ} with 0≤r≤1; q≥2 makes H(θ)=(1+r²+2r cosθ)^{q/2}+(1+r²−2r cosθ)^{q/2} decrease on [0,π/2] by the explicit derivative −qr sinθ[(1+r²+2r cosθ)^{q/2−1}−(1+r²−2r cosθ)^{q/2−1}]≤0. Symmetry reduces all θ to this interval, so the aligned real case is maximal. Apply the scalar estimate pointwise to f,g. Minkowski in the two-dimensional ℓ_{q/p} space, applied to the nonnegative vector (|f+g|^p,|f−g|^p), yields (||f+g||_p^q+||f−g||_p^q)^{p/q}≤∫(|f+g|^q+|f−g|^q)^{p/q}≤2^{p/q}(||f||_p^p+||g||_p^p). Raise to q/p and divide by 2^q. The p=2 formulas coincide. Every integral is finite because f,g∈L^p. This route uses only real calculus, finite-dimensional Minkowski, and the declared nonnegative integral rules.
items.statement: Let 1<p<infinity. For p>=2, ||(f+g)/2||_p^p+||(f-g)/2||_p^p <= (||f||_p^p+||g||_p^p)/2. For 1<p<=2 and q=p/(p-1), the sum of the q-th powers of those two midpoint norms is at most ((||f||_p^p+||g||_p^p)/2)^(q/p), over both real and complex scalars.

references.title: Kuriyama, Miyagi, Okada and Miyoshi, Elementary proof of Clarkson’s inequalities and their generalization, Theorems 2.5, 3.2 and 3.4, pp. 120–124

items.title: Lp is uniformly convex for one less p less infinity
items.strategy: For ||f||_p,||g||_p≤1 and ||f−g||_p≥ε∈(0,2], put m=(f+g)/2 and d=(f−g)/2. If p≥2, Clarkson gives ||m||_p^p+||d||_p^p≤1, hence ||m||_p≤(1−(ε/2)^p)^{1/p}. If 1<p≤2, with q=p/(p−1), its second inequality gives ||m||_p^q+||d||_p^q≤1, hence ||m||_p≤(1−(ε/2)^q)^{1/q}. Both yield an explicit strictly positive modulus δ(ε)=1 minus the displayed bound, including ε=2. The real and complex cases are covered by the same preceding scalar inequalities.
items.statement: Assume countable choice. For 1<p<infinity, real and complex scalar Lp spaces with their usual norms are uniformly convex.

items.title: Real and complex c zero are Banach
items.strategy: For a supremum-norm Cauchy sequence in c0, every coordinate is Cauchy in the scalar field and therefore has a unique limit. Replacement collects these uniquely specified limits into one scalar sequence, so no choice principle is used. A fixed Cauchy tail gives a uniform bound and uniform convergence to the coordinatewise limit; comparison with one fixed null sequence proves that the limit still tends to zero. Thus c0 is complete for the supremum norm over both real and complex scalars.
items.statement: For either real or complex scalars, c0 with the supremum norm is a Banach space. No choice principle is used.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis, Problem 4.17(i), printed p. 118

items.title: Hilbert spaces are uniformly convex
items.strategy: Define a Hilbert space locally as an inner-product space complete for the induced norm, using the already published inner-product definition; this is an inline specialization, not a forward FA-13 supplier. Expand ||x+y||² and ||x−y||² by linearity and conjugate symmetry to prove the parallelogram identity for real and complex scalars. For ||x||,||y||≤1 and ||x−y||≥ε, it gives ||(x+y)/2||²=(||x||²+||y||²)/2−||x−y||²/4≤1−ε²/4. Hence δ(ε)=1−sqrt(1−ε²/4)>0 for 0<ε≤2. Cauchy–Schwarz supplies the induced norm, and completeness makes it a Banach-space example. No later Hilbert theorem is invoked.
items.statement: Every real or complex Hilbert space is uniformly convex; the parallelogram identity gives the explicit modulus delta(epsilon)=1-sqrt(1-epsilon^2/4).

items.title: Reflexivity of ell p and lp
items.strategy: For 1<p<infinity apply the real-or-complex arbitrary-measure reflexivity theorem, with counting measure giving ell-p through the published counting-measure identification. Record the endpoints separately: the closed c0 subspace and the HB closed-subspace theorem rule out reflexivity of ell-infinity, while counting measure identifies it with L-infinity. Do not infer an endpoint assertion for every measure space.
items.statement: Assume countable choice. For 1<p<infinity, real and complex ell-p and Lp over arbitrary measure spaces are reflexive. Real and complex c0 are not reflexive. Under the additional ultrafilter lemma, DC and relative Hahn-Banach assumptions, real and complex ell-one and ell-infinity are not reflexive; counting measure makes ell-infinity an L-infinity endpoint counterexample.

items.title: C0 is not reflexive
items.strategy: Under the sourced bilinear sequence dualities the canonical map is c0 inclusion into ell-infinity; the constant-one sequence is not in its image. For the real ell-one dual use the real counting-measure corollary, not the complex-only theorem.
items.statement: Real and complex c0 are not reflexive.

items.title: Weak and norm topologies differ on ell one despite identical convergent sequences
items.strategy: Every basic weak neighborhood of zero contains a nonzero common-kernel vector of its finitely many functionals and all its multiples; it cannot lie in a norm ball. Schur nevertheless identifies convergent sequences. Verify finite-codimension kernel existence inline.
items.statement: On infinite-dimensional ell-one the weak and norm topologies differ, although by the Schur theorem they have exactly the same convergent sequences.

items.title: Complex bishop phelps for general convex sets
items.strategy: Recorded source boundary only. Summarize Lomonosov's Theorem 2 and never use this remark as a dependency.
items.statement: Lomonosov constructed a complex Banach space and a closed bounded convex subset with no support points, so the real general-convex Bishop-Phelps theorem has no unrestricted complex analogue; the complex unit-ball case remains valid under the declared DC and relative-HB hypotheses of the local theorem.

references.title: Victor Lomonosov, A Counterexample to the Bishop-Phelps Theorem in Complex Spaces
references.locator: Theorem 1, pp.3-4, and Theorem 2, pp.4-5, of the five-page paper

external_dependency.exact_statement: There is a complex Banach space X1 and a closed bounded convex subset S1 for which only the zero functional attains its maximum modulus; hence S1 has no support points.
external_dependency.local_proof_attempt: The source uses the predual of H-infinity, maximum-modulus powers, RMK on a maximal ideal space, and a quotient by point evaluation; these prerequisites are not developed locally here.
external_dependency.necessity: The design requires the warning that the general real closed-bounded-convex theorem does not extend to complex spaces. This remark is non-load-bearing.

items.title: Norm attaining functionals on a hilbert space
items.strategy: Give a local Riesz proof from the published inner-product definition, rather than citing the later FA-13 theorem. A Hilbert space is a complete inner-product space. For a nonzero bounded linear f choose v with f(v)=1; M=ker f is closed and complete. Let d=inf_{m∈M}||v−m||>0 and, using the declared countable choice assumption, select m_n with ||v−m_n||→d. The parallelogram identity applied to v−m_n and v−m_k shows ||m_n−m_k||²≤2||v−m_n||²+2||v−m_k||²−4d²→0, since (m_n+m_k)/2∈M. Thus m_n→m∈M. Set z=v−m≠0. Expanding ||z−t u||²≥||z||² for all u∈M and real t, and also imaginary t in the complex case, proves z⊥M. Because x−f(x)z∈M, linear-first convention gives f(x)=<x,z>/||z||². Cauchy–Schwarz yields ||f||=1/||z||, attained at z/||z||. The zero functional attains its norm at every unit-ball point. This proof supplies the complete local geometric argument and does not import James or a forward FA-13 item.
items.statement: Assume countable choice. Every bounded linear functional on a real or complex Hilbert space attains its norm on the closed unit ball; a nonzero functional has a unique representing vector y and attains its norm at y/||y||, while the zero functional is represented by zero and attains its norm everywhere on the ball.

references.title: Theo Bühler and Dietmar A. Salamon, Functional Analysis
Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis
